'''''Chelidonium majus''''', the '''greater celandine''', is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous]] [[flowering plant]] in the poppy family [[Papaveraceae]]. One of two species in the genus ''[[Chelidonium]]'', it is native to Europe and western Asia and [[introduced species|introduced]] widely in North America.

The plant known as lesser celandine (''[[Ficaria verna]]'') is not closely related, as it belongs to the buttercup family Ranunculaceae.

==Description==
Greater celandine is a perennial herbaceous plant with an erect habit, and reaches {{convert|30|-|120|cm|abbr=on}} high. The blue-green<ref name="Reader's Digest-1981" /> leaves are [[pinnate]] with lobed and wavy margins, up to {{convert|30|cm|abbr=on}} long. When injured, the plant exudes a yellow to orange [[latex]].<ref name="Reader's Digest-1981" /><ref name="Stace-2019">{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2019|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Fourth|publisher=C & M Floristics|location = Middlewood Green, Suffolk, U.K.| isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>{{rp|96}}

The flowers consist of four yellow petals, each about {{convert|18|mm|abbr=on}} long, with two [[sepal]]s. A double-flowered variety occurs naturally. The flowers appear from late spring to summer, May to September (in the UK),<ref name="Reader's Digest-1981">{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=30 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=978-0-276-00217-5}}</ref> in [[umbelliform]] [[cyme (botany)|cymes]] of about four flowers.

The seeds are small and black, borne in a long, cylindrical [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]]. Each has an [[elaiosome]], which attracts ants to disperse the seeds ([[myrmecochory]]).<ref name="Reader's Digest-1981" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Chelidonium majus'' was described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in volume one of his ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753.<ref>{{cite book |author=Linnaeus C |title=Species Plantarum|publisher=Laurentii Salvii |location=Stockholm |year=1753|chapter=Tomus I |volume=1|page=505|chapter-url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358524 |language=la}}</ref> It is classified in the genus ''[[Chelidonium]]'' within the wider family [[Papaveraceae]]. It has two accepted [[subspecies]].<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |id=303589-2 |title=''Chelidonium majus'' L. |access-date=16 December 2025}}</ref>

* ''Chelidonium majus'' subsp. ''grandiflorum'' – Native to Siberia, China, and Korea<ref name="POWO subsp grandiflorum">{{cite POWO |id=77249467-1 |title=''Chelidonium majus'' subsp. ''grandiflorum'' (DC.) Printz |access-date=16 December 2025}}</ref>
* ''Chelidonium majus'' subsp. ''majus'' – Native to Europe, western Asia, and a small area of North Africa<ref name="POWO subsp majus">{{cite POWO |id=77228693-1 |title=''Chelidonium majus'' subsp. ''majus'' |access-date=16 December 2025}}</ref>

There are a total of {{table row counter|id=Synonyms}} [[Synonym (botany)|synonyms]] of its two subspecies including eleven species names.<ref name="POWO subsp grandiflorum" /><ref name="POWO subsp majus" />

The name ''celandine'' comes from [[Late Latin]] ''celidonia'', from earlier Latin ''chelidonia'' or ''chelidonium'', and ultimately from [[Ancient Greek]] {{lang|grc|χελιδόνιον}}, from {{lang|grc|χελιδών}} (''chelidṓn'') '[[swallow]]', hence the common name ''swallowwort''. Ancient writers said that the flower bloomed when the swallows returned and faded when they left.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://dictionary.oed.com/cgi/entry/50035272 |title=Swallow |work=Oxford English Dictionary, Second Edition |year=1989 |publisher=Oxford University Press, Oxford}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Hanzlik, P.J. |year=1920 |title=The pharmacology of chelidonin, a neglected alkaloid of chelidonium, or tetterwort |journal=Journal of the American Medical Association |volume=75 |issue=20 |pages=1324–1325 |doi=10.1001/jama.1920.02620460022007}}</ref>  ''Chelidonium majus'' has also been called ''great celandine'',{{r|grin}} ''nipplewort'',{{r|grin}} ''tetterwort'',<ref name="Xu-2016">{{cite book | last=Xu | first=J.P. | title=Cancer Inhibitors from Chinese Natural Medicines | publisher=CRC Press | year=2016 | isbn=978-1-4987-8766-6 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K-mVDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA441 | access-date=2023-08-23 | page=441}}</ref> or simply ''celandine''.{{r|grin}} The common name ''tetterwort'' also refers to ''[[Sanguinaria canadensis]]''.<ref name="Predny-2005">{{cite book | last1=Predny | first1=M.L. | last2=Chamberlain | first2=J.L. | author3=United States. National Park Service | title=Bloodroot (Sanguinaria Canadensis): An Annotated Bibliography | publisher=U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Southern Research Station | series=General technical report SRS | year=2005 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CQPxAAAAMAAJ | access-date=2023-08-23 | page=}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Chelidonium majus'' is [[native plant|native]] to most regions of Europe. It is also found in North Africa in [[Macaronesia]], [[Algeria]] and [[Morocco]]. In Western Asia it is found in the [[Caucasus]], [[Armenia]], [[Azerbaijan]], [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], [[Kazakhstan]], [[Mongolia]], [[Siberia]], [[Iran]] and [[Turkey]].{{r|grin}} Its habitats include rocky slopes, woodlands, waste areas and roadsides.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chelidonium majus - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=284857 |access-date=2024-03-30 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref>

==Ecology==
It is considered an aggressive invasive plant in parts of North America and an invasive plant in other areas. In [[Wisconsin]], for example, it is a restricted plant.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chapter NR 40 INVASIVE SPECIES IDENTIFICATION, CLASSIFICATION AND CONTROL|url=http://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/code/admin_code/nr/001/40.pdf|publisher=wisconsin.gov|access-date=3 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eddmaps.org/ipane/ipanespecies/herbs/Chelidonium_majus.htm |title=Invasive Plant Atlas of New England |access-date=2015-06-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150730220930/http://www.eddmaps.org/ipane/ipanespecies/herbs/Chelidonium_majus.htm |archive-date=2015-07-30 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Control is obtained mainly via pulling or spraying the plant before seed dispersal.

==Commercial uses==

The yellow sap of plant is used in small quantities for a yellow-orange craft dye, and as an imitation gold paint<ref name="Orange dyes - Cambridge University Botanic Garden 2026">{{Cite web|url=https://www.botanic.cam.ac.uk/collections/botanic-dyes/orange-dyes-2/|title = Orange Dyes / Chelidonium majus}}</ref>. 

==Constituents and pharmacology==
[[File:Chelidonium majus sap 3 AB.jpg|thumb|A cut stem exuding yellow latex]]
The whole plant is toxic in moderate doses as it contains a range of [[isoquinoline alkaloids]]; use in herbal medicine requires the correct dose.<ref name="Gruenwald-2000">{{cite book |first=Joerg |last=Gruenwald |title=PDR for Herbal Medicines |publisher=Thomson PDR |year=2000 |isbn=978-1-56363-361-4 |url=https://archive.org/details/pdrforherbalmedi00joer }}</ref> The main alkaloid present in the [[herb]] and [[root]] is [[coptisine]]. Other alkaloids present include methyl 2'-(7,8-dihydrosanguinarine-8-yl)acetate, [[allocryptopine]],<ref>Cahlikova L., Opletal L., Kurfurst M., Macakova K., Kulhankova A., Host'alkova A.,"Acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase inhibitory compounds from Chelidonium majus (Papaveraceae)."  ''Natural Product Communications''. 5 (11) (pp 1751–1754), 2010. Date of Publication: 2010.</ref> [[stylopine]], [[protopine]], cryptopine, hemochelidonine, homochelidonine, [[norchelidonine]], [[berberine]], [[chelidonine]], [[sanguinarine]], [[chelerythrine]]<ref>Li X.-L., Yao J.-Y., Zhou Z.-M., Shen J.-Y., Ru H.-S., Liu X.-L.,"Activity of the chelerythrine, a quaternary benzo[c]phenanthridine alkaloid from Chelidonium majus L. on Dactylogyrus intermedius." ''Parasitology Research''. 109 (1) (pp 247-252), July 2011</ref> and [[8-hydroxydihydrosanguinarine]].<ref>Park J.E., Cuong T.D., Hung T.M., Lee I., Na M., Kim J.C., Ryoo S., Lee J.H., Choi J.S., Woo M.H., Min B.S.,"Alkaloids from Chelidonium majus and their inhibitory effects on LPS-induced NO production in RAW264.7 cells".  ''Bioorganic & Medicinal Chemistry Letters''. 21 (23) (pp 6960-6963), 2011. Date of Publication: 01 Dec 2011.</ref> Sanguinarine is particularly toxic with an {{LD50}} of 18 mg per kg body weight (IP in rats).<ref>{{cite book |last=Golob |first=Peter |author2=Caroline Moss |author3=Melanie Dales |author4=Alex Fidgen |author5=Jenny Evans |author6=Irene Gudrups |title=The use of spices and medicinals as bioactive protectants for grains |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/x2230e/x2230e00.htm |access-date=2008-07-17 |series=FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin |volume=137 |year=1999 |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization]] |location=[[Rome]] |isbn=978-92-5-104294-6}}</ref> [[Caffeic acid]] derivatives, such as [[caffeoylmalic acid]], are also present.<ref>{{cite journal |pmid=17230338|year=1993|last1=Hahn|first1=R.|title=Hydroxycinnamic Acid Derivatives, Caffeoylmalic and New Caffeoylaldonic Acid Esters, from Chelidonium majus*,1|journal=Planta Medica|volume=59|issue=1|pages=71–5|last2=Nahrstedt|first2=A.|doi=10.1055/s-2006-959608|bibcode=1993PlMed..59...71H |s2cid=21131585 }}</ref>

The characteristic latex also contains [[proteolytic enzymes]] and the phyto[[cystatin]] [[chelidostatin]], a [[cysteine protease]] inhibitor.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rogelj |first1=B. |year=1998 |title=Chelidocystatin, a novel phytocystatin from Chelidonium majus|journal=Phytochemistry |volume=49 |issue=6|pages=1645–9 |pmid=9862139 |doi=10.1016/s0031-9422(98)00281-7|bibcode=1998PChem..49.1645R |display-authors=etal}}</ref> It is a traditional folk remedy against [[wart]]s in France,<ref>[https://www.sciencesetavenir.fr/sante/video-la-chelidoine-une-plante-contre-la-verrue_30991 La chélidoine, une plante contre la verrue dans Science et avenir 2016]</ref> German-speaking countries,<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.onmeda.de/krankheiten/warzen/schoellkraut-warzen-id202756/ | title=Hilft Schöllkraut gegen Warzen? | date=13 December 2021 }}</ref> Hungary,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Izabella |first=Simon |date=2021-02-14 |title=Szemölcsre: vérehulló fecskefű! |trans-title=For warts: bleeding swallowwort! |url=https://www.hazipatika.com/eletmod/termeszetes_gyogymodok/cikkek/szemolcsre_verehullo_fecskefu |website=Hazipatika |language=hu}}</ref> and the UK. It is used in the preparation of a range of off-the-shelf treatments for warts and skin conditions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wildflowerfinder.org.uk/Flowers/C/Celandine(Greater)/Celandine(Greater).htm|title = Celandine (Greater) / Greater Celandine - Wild Flower Finder}}</ref>



''Chelidonium'' is used to make [[Ukrain]], a drug that has been promoted for the treatment of cancer and viral infections but is not known to be effective.<ref name="American Cancer Society-2011">{{cite web|title=Celandine|publisher=[[American Cancer Society]]|date=August 2011|access-date=5 September 2013|url=http://www.cancer.org/treatment/treatmentsandsideeffects/complementaryandalternativemedicine/herbsvitaminsandminerals/celandine|archive-date=23 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150423221233/http://www.cancer.org/treatment/treatmentsandsideeffects/complementaryandalternativemedicine/herbsvitaminsandminerals/celandine|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Ernst-2012">{{cite web |url=http://edzardernst.com/2012/10/a-telling-story-about-alternative-cancer-cures-and-their-purveyors/ |title=A telling story about "alternative" cancer cures and their purveyors |date=14 October 2012 |access-date=December 4, 2012 |author=Edzard Ernst |author-link=Edzard Ernst }}</ref>

The fresh herb is no longer used officially. No dose-finding studies exist and the reported clinical studies are characterised by a considerable heterogeneity.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=European Medicines Agency |title=Assessment report on Chelidonium majus L., herba |date=September 13, 2011 |url=https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/herbal-report/final-assessment-report-chelidonium-majus-l-herba_en.pdf}}</ref>

Except for homeopathic medicines, the drug is no longer used in most English-speaking countries. In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, extracts of Chelidoni herba are a controversial component of the gastric remedy Iberogast. The OTC-preparation is a top-selling product for the company [[Bayer]], which is now under investigation for not warning consumers of possible hepatotoxic side-effects when taking the drug. Elevated liver-enzymes and toxic hepatitis with a documented fatality have been reported.<ref>F. Pantano, G. Mannocchi, E. Marinelli, S. Gentili, S. Graziano, F.P. Busardò, N.M. di Luca
[https://www.europeanreview.org/article/12431 "Hepatotoxicity induced by greater celandine (Chelidonium majus L.): a review of the literature."] Eur Rev Med Pharmacol Sci 2017; 21 (1 Suppl): 46-52. Retrieved 21 July 2019</ref><ref>Aiolfi S (July 2019). [https://www.nzz.ch/wirtschaft/bayer-medikament-im-fokus-der-staatsanwaltschaft-ld.1497375 Bayer-Medikament im Fokus der Staatsanwaltschaft](in German). Neue Zürcher Zeitung. Retrieved 21 July 2019.</ref>

The plant is poisonous to chickens.<ref name="Niering-1985">{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering|last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=671}}</ref>

==Herbalism==
The aerial parts and roots of greater celandine are used in [[Herbal medicine|herbalism]]. The above-ground parts are gathered during the flowering season and dried at high temperatures. The root is harvested in autumn between August and October and dried. The fresh rhizome is also used. Celandine has a hot and bitter taste. Preparations are made from [[ethanol|alcoholic]] and hot aqueous extractions. The related plant [[bloodroot]] has similar chemical composition and uses to greater celandine.

As far back as [[Pliny the Elder]] and [[Dioscorides]] (1st century CE), this herb has erroneously been seen as a detoxifying agent. The root has been chewed to relieve toothache.<ref>{{cite book |first=Andrew |last=Chevallier |title=The encyclopedia of medicinal plants |publisher=DK Publishing |location=New York |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-7894-1067-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofme00chev/page/185 185] |url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofme00chev/page/185 }}</ref> [[John Gerard]]'s ''Herball'' (1597) states that "the juice of the herbe is good to sharpen the sight, for it cleanseth and consumeth away slimie things that cleave about the ball of the eye and hinder the sight and especially being boiled with honey in a brasen vessell."<ref>{{cite book|title=A Modern Herbal: The Medicinal, Culinary, Cosmetic and Economic Properties, Cultivation and Folk-lore of Herbs, Grasses, Fungi, Shrubs, & Trees with All Their Modern Scientific Uses, Volume 1|author=Grieve, Maud|year=1971}}</ref>

It was formerly used by some [[Romani people]] as a foot refresher; modern herbalists use its [[purgative]] properties.<ref>{{cite book |last=Howard |first=Michael |title=Traditional Folk Remedies |series=Century Paperbacks |date=1987-05-21 |publisher=Ebury Press |isbn=978-0-7126-1731-4 |pages=146–147}}</ref>
The modern [[herbalist]] [[Juliette de Baïracli Levy]] recommended greater celandine diluted with milk for the eyes and the latex for getting rid of warts.<ref>Bailes M., "The Healing Garden", {{ISBN|978-0-7318-0753-6}}</ref> ''Chelidonium'' was a favourite herb of the French herbalist [[Maurice Mességué]].
''Chelidonium majus'' has traditionally been used for treatment of various inflammatory diseases including [[atopic dermatitis]].<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Gabsik Yang |author2=Kyungjin Lee |author3=Mi-Hwa Lee |author4=So-Hyung Kim |author5=In-Hye Ham |author6=Ho-Young Choi |year=2011 |title=Inhibitory effects of ''Chelidonium majus'' extract on atopic dermatitis-like skin lesions in NC/Nga mice |journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |volume=138 |issue=2 |pages=398–403 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2011.09.028 |pmid=21963561}}</ref> It is also traditionally used in the treatment of gallstones and dyspepsia.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Gabriela Mazzanti |author2=Antonella di Sotto |author3=Antonio Franchitto |author4=Caterina Loredana Mammola |author5=Paola Mariani |author6=Sabina Mastrangelo |author7=Francesca Menniti-Ippolito |author8=Annabella Vitalone |year=2009 |title=''Chelidonium majus'' is not hepatotoxic in Wistar rats, in a 4 weeks feeding experiment |journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |volume=126 |issue=3 |pages=518–524 |pmid=19761826 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2009.09.004}}</ref>

The [[Iroquois]] give an [[infusion]] of the whole plant, another plant and milk to pigs that drool and exhibit sudden movements.<ref>Rousseau, Jacques 1945 Le Folklore Botanique De Caughnawaga. Contributions de l'Institut botanique l'Universite de Montreal 55:7-72 (p. 45)</ref>{{Clarify|reason=unclear sentence phrasing—which other plant? what are sudden movements?|date=December 2019}}

It was also once used to treat liver disorders, owing to the juice's resemblance to bile.<ref name="Niering-1985"/> However, ingesting plant may actually lead to [[hepatotoxicity]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548684/ | pmid=31643995 | date=2012 | title=Greater Celandine | publisher=National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases }}</ref>
